A fictional education cooperative asks you to specify the single best curriculum for children who will become adults in a society whose technologies and institutions may change substantially. Families disagree about what a good education is, yet the cooperative must choose what to teach next term. Give a recommendation it can act on and explain how it could discover that the recommendation was mistaken.

END PROBLEM

{"answer":"The best curriculum the cooperative can adopt next term is a common adaptive core of transferable capabilities—literacy, numeracy, scientific and civic reasoning, learning-to-learn, ethical deliberation, collaboration, arts, health, and practical life skills—delivered through structured projects and elective pathways, with transparent governance and longitudinal falsification checks. Concretely, it should teach foundational language and mathematics; inquiry in science, history, and civics; critical thinking and metacognitive learning strategies; collaborative problem solving; moral and civic deliberation; arts and physical education; and practical life skills such as budgeting, cooking, basic repair, and digital literacy. It should use project-based and community-linked work, reserve time for electives chosen by families and students, and keep a common core that no family can be excluded from. To discover whether this recommendation is mistaken, the cooperative should predefine indicators: graduates' ability to learn new tools and institutions, critical-thinking and civic-participation measures, wellbeing, employment/education pathways, and family/student feedback. It should compare variants through randomized or quasi-experimental assignment where ethical, track cohorts longitudinally, and publish results. The recommendation is mistaken if graduates systematically fail to adapt, if the core harms or excludes particular groups, or if a feasible alternative reliably outperforms it on these agreed measures;
